title: Core Data Concepts – New Notes
subtitle: Episode 1: core data concepts and Azure services — the foundation for the rest of DP-900.

what.body: This session builds the foundation for the whole DP-900: which data formats exist, how files and databases store data, how transactional and analytical workloads differ, who works with data, and which Azure service each role reaches for.
what.example: A business tracks customers, products and orders (entities with attributes like name, address, phone). It collects that data, processes it, and uses the outcomes — e.g. a predefined sales table for daily operations.

concepts.body: Follows a defined schema: every record uses the same fields and types. Easy to store, search and analyze. Example: a sales table with fixed columns.

Organized but flexible — records may carry different attributes. Often name–value pairs like JSON, where one record has email + phone and another only email. Flexible and compact, but needs extra logic to process.
No predefined fields or schema; stored as files. Examples: documents, images, audio, video — each file is one item. Easy to store, harder to query without extra processing.
Plain text, one row per line, commas or tabs separate columns. Works well for structured lists like products, customers and logs.
Hierarchical objects with nested objects and collections. Great for optional or varying fields; used in web apps, templates and login systems.
Text with markup tags describing each value. Still found in older systems and industry integrations, but less common than JSON.
Binary Large Objects: Word docs, PDFs, images, videos. Each BLOB is an independent object (often a block blob) in Blob storage.
Row-based compact binary with a small JSON header describing the schema. Efficient for storage and network transfer.
Columnar formats with indexing, statistics and metadata. Engines like Hive skip unneeded chunks, so analytics over huge datasets runs far faster. Parquet also handles nested types well.
Structured data in tables for entities (customer, product, orders). Each instance has a primary key; foreign keys link tables. Normalization removes duplication, and everything is managed with SQL.

Flexible, non-relational stores: key-value (unique key + value), document (key + JSON document the engine can query), column-family (related column groups), graph (nodes + relationships, best when connections matter most).
Runs live business systems — order entry, payments. Optimized for frequent reads/writes where each transaction updates operational state and must stay accurate and consistent.
Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (one valid state to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), Durability (committed work survives failures).
Understands the business instead of running it: trends, comparisons and patterns like month-over-month sales. Aggregates data and reads huge volumes for reporting and decisions.
Extract from operational (OLTP) sources, Transform (clean and reshape), Load into a dedicated analytical environment so analysis never slows production.
Huge volumes of raw data in files. In Azure: Data Lake Storage Gen2.
Structured data in relational tables for analytics. In Azure: Synapse Analytics, Microsoft Fabric Warehouse.
Lake flexibility plus warehouse-style tabular structure and transactions. In Azure: Fabric Lakehouse, Databricks Lakehouse.
Multi-dimensional models (time, product, region) with precomputed totals and comparisons, so dashboards answer instantly without recalculating.
Keeps databases reliable, secure and available: provisioning, access/security, backups and recovery, performance monitoring. Focus: operational and relational systems.
Moves and prepares data: builds pipelines and ETL so data lands in lakes, lakehouses and warehouses in the right place, format and time.
Works with prepared data to build analytical models, reports and dashboards that reveal trends for decisions.
Scientists do advanced analytics and machine learning; architects design the overall data platform and structure. Awareness-level for DP-900.

examples.title: One record, three formats
examples.body: The same customer in CSV (flat row), JSON (nested address object) and a table row — shape changes, facts don't.

examples.title: From OLTP to OLAP
examples.body: Nightly ETL copies orders out of the live SQL database, cleans them, and loads a warehouse — Monday's trend report never touches Friday's checkout queue.

examples.title: Pick the analytical store
examples.body: Raw files at scale → lake. Structured relational analytics → warehouse. Lake files plus SQL tables with transactions → lakehouse.

services.name: Azure SQL Database
services.when: App databases with no server management.

services.name: Azure SQL Managed Instance
services.what: PaaS with higher SQL Server compatibility.
services.when: Migrating SQL Server workloads mostly unchanged.

services.name: SQL Server on Azure VM
services.when: You need full customization and accept the management.
services.scenario: A legacy app needing exact version behavior.

services.name: MariaDB / MySQL / PostgreSQL
services.scenario: A Django app that only speaks PostgreSQL.

services.name: Azure Cosmos DB
services.data: Semi-structured and flexible data at scale.
services.scenario: Product catalogs served on every continent.

services.name: Azure Storage + Data Lake
services.what: Files, blobs, tables and lake storage.
services.data: Unstructured files and raw analytic data.
services.scenario: Years of clickstream logs awaiting analysis.

services.name: Microsoft Fabric
services.what: SaaS analytics platform in one place.
services.data: Ingestion, lakehouse, warehouse, ML, real-time, visualization.
services.when: One SaaS suite instead of many wired services.
services.scenario: A team wanting pipelines, warehouse, Spark and Power BI together.

services.name: Azure Databricks
services.scenario: Training models over terabytes of logs.

services.name: Microsoft Purview
services.when: Mapping data and applying policies consistently.
services.scenario: Finding every dataset holding customer PII.

remember: Fixed rows/columns → structured · JSON/XML flexible → semi-structured · media/files → unstructured.
Columnar formats (ORC, Parquet) exist for analytics speed at scale.
ETL copies from OLTP, cleans, and loads a separate analytical store.
Raw files → lake · relational analytics → warehouse · lake + SQL tables → lakehouse.
Backup/recovery → DBA · ETL pipelines → Data Engineer · reports/dashboards → Data Analyst.
SaaS analytics with lakehouse + warehouse + real-time + Power BI → Microsoft Fabric.

quickCheck.q: Optional email/phone fields in JSON records: which type?
quickCheck.a: Semi-structured — organized but varying by record.

quickCheck.q: Hourly fraud checks on live payments: OLTP or OLAP?
Which ACID property survives a power cut after commit?
Raw logs now, unknown analysis later: lake or warehouse?
quickCheck.a: Data lake — raw files at scale.
